summary:
Tumbes stands under Peru's national framework: trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. There is no documented local mitigation for this border department, and the national restroom rule applies to public facilities including transport hubs, which matters because the bill was triggered by a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions cover custody situations, places where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; the package also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', subject to narrow listed exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries this mandate, so trans people including trans youth are barred from facilities matching their gender identity.

The legal analysis of IDEHPUCP at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte dated 15 April 2025, argues that article 5 directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP has separately found the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people and has recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Practical enforcement is expected to rest on front-line staff. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warned that bathroom access would come to depend on security personnel's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private life as well: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Because identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation and legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, an ID check at a restroom door or a border checkpoint carries a concrete risk of outing. Peru's entry and screening arrangements are national, and nothing in the sources documents a Tumbes-specific carve-out.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. That binding regional standard sits against the April 2025 statute, and the Inter-American framework also underlay the Rojas Marín litigation.
tangentialFactors:
Speech and association are constrained alongside facility access. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Two protective developments are on record and cut against the prevailing direction. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

The national pattern is measurable in comparative terms: after the 2017 repeal Peru stands with Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American states without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, a regional outlier position that shapes what protection a trans traveller can expect from police and prosecutors.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tumbes are governed by the same national restroom statute as visitors, but the practical burden falls harder on those who live and work in the department: daily use of workplaces, shops, malls, hospitals and municipal buildings now turns on the 'biological sex' test in article 5, with no documented departmental ordinance softening it.

Legal gender recognition for residents remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents held by trans people in Tumbes frequently still carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation, which is what exposes them to document checks at facilities and at the border crossing into Ecuador.

Healthcare access for trans residents improved at the level of national guidance in June 2024, when health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official instructions; implementation at regional hospitals in Tumbes is not sourced here.

Residents have access to the national complaint machinery: the constitutional and Inter-American routes used by IDEHPUCP litigants, and the consumer-protection body whose handling of a gym complaint shows the limits of administrative remedy.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tumbes-specific enforcement data is sourced: the inventory contains no record of how many times article 5 has been invoked in this department, no local police instructions, and no reported incident of a trans person being refused a restroom, checked for ID, or removed from a facility in Tumbes.

The claim that enforcement is 'expected to reach transport hubs' is an inference from the law's national scope and its airport-signage origin, not a sourced observation of practice at Tumbes airport or the Aguas Verdes border post; this remains unresolved.

Whether the exceptions in the February 2025 dictamen survived verbatim into the statute proclaimed in April 2025 is not fully resolved by the sources: IDEHPUCP describes 'narrow listed exceptions' without enumerating them, and the enumerated list comes from the committee-stage text.

Current caseload figures for legal gender recognition proceedings, and any Tumbes court's handling of a recognition petition, are not sourced in this inventory.

Local facility inventory for trans visitors, including availability of single-occupancy or all-gender restrooms in Tumbes hotels, the port and the airport, is not sourced.
